issues.legal_issue: The length of delay alone does not determine whether delay should be condoned; the acceptability of the explanation is the controlling consideration.
material_facts: An application to restore a proceeding dismissed for default was filed 883 days after the dismissal.
The applicant said his advocate had not informed him of the dismissal and that he learned of it after receiving execution-related process.
The trial court accepted the explanation and condoned the delay.
issues.conclusion: The length of the delay did not itself prevent condonation; an acceptable explanation may justify condoning even a very long delay, while a short delay may be refused if its explanation is unacceptable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, “sufficient cause” is construed liberally to advance substantial justice. The length of delay is not decisive; the acceptability of the explanation is. Delay should not be condoned where the explanation is mala fide or part of a dilatory strategy. The Court relied on Shakuntala Devi Jain v. Kuntal Kumari, AIR 1969 SC 575, and State of West Bengal v. The Administrator, Howrah Municipality, AIR 1972 SC 749.

rule.if: delay_condonation_application and explanation_is_acceptable and not explanation_is_mala_fide_or_dilatory

predicates.delay_condonation_application: A party applied to have a delayed proceeding or filing accepted.
predicates.explanation_is_acceptable: The court found the applicant’s account of the delay satisfactory.
predicates.explanation_is_mala_fide_or_dilatory: The explanation was shown to be dishonest or offered as a strategy to gain time.

issues.definition: When a party seeks condonation, the delay is condoned if the court accepts the explanation and it is not mala fide or dilatory.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court should not disturb a lower court’s discretionary decision to condone delay unless that decision rests on untenable grounds or is arbitrary or perverse.
material_facts: The trial court accepted the explanation for the delay and exercised its discretion to condone it.
The High Court, in revision, reversed that decision because it considered the applicant insufficiently diligent in checking on the proceeding.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had wrongly upset the trial court’s exercise of discretion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have set aside the trial court’s order in revision; the trial court’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Once a court has accepted an explanation and exercised its discretion to condone delay, a superior court should normally not disturb that decision, particularly in revisional jurisdiction, unless the exercise was on wholly untenable grounds or was arbitrary or perverse. If the lower court refuses condonation, a superior court may consider the explanation afresh.

predicates.revision_against_delay_condonation: A party sought revisional review of a lower court’s decision to condone delay.
predicates.lower_court_accepted_explanation: The lower court found the applicant’s explanation satisfactory and condoned the delay.
predicates.lower_court_exercise_arbitrary_perverse_: The lower court’s exercise of discretion was arbitrary, perverse, or based on wholly untenable grounds.

issues.definition: On revision of a decision condoning delay, the decision is left undisturbed when the lower court accepted the explanation and its exercise of discretion was not arbitrary, perverse, or untenable.

issues.legal_issue: An opposing party should be compensated when delay is condoned despite the applicant’s laches and the opposing party has incurred litigation expense.
material_facts: The applicant’s conduct included a failure to check the progress of the proceeding for a long period.
The opposing party had incurred litigation expenses.
The applicant had also obtained compensation from the advocate whose conduct contributed to the delay.
The Supreme Court restored condonation on the condition that the applicant compensate the opposing party.
issues.conclusion: The applicant was required to compensate the opposing party as a condition of restoring the order condoning delay.
issues.legal_principle: When delay is condoned because of the applicant’s laches, the court should not overlook the opposing party’s loss and litigation expenses; compensation is a salutary guideline. The Court applied that principle by making compensation a condition of restoring the trial court’s order.

predicates.delay_condonation_proceeding: A court considered whether to condone delay in a proceeding.
predicates.applicant_laches_contributed_to_delay: The applicant’s lack of diligence contributed to the delay.
predicates.opposing_party_incurred_litigation_expen: The opposing party incurred expenses in the litigation affected by the delay.

issues.definition: When a delay-condonation proceeding involves applicant laches and litigation expense to the opposing party, the opposing party is compensated.
